assertions.evidence: The response contains two markdown tables: 'Shipping Method Availability' and 'Shipping Cost Calculation', both formatted as markdown tables with pipe-delimited columns and headers.

assertions.text: Express shipping is split into at least two cases distinguishing the UK free tier (UK, order £50+, free) from the paid tier. The split is driven by the UK-only free threshold rule.
assertions.evidence: The cost table contains separate rows for: 'Express – exactly at threshold, UK (free tier)' with UK at £50 = £0.00, 'Express – above threshold, UK' with UK at £75 = £0.00, and 'Express – at or above threshold, non-UK (no free tier)' with {Ireland, EU, International} at {£50, £75} = £9.99. This clearly distinguishes UK free tier from non-UK paid tier above threshold.

assertions.text: Express rows use value sets to consolidate cases with the same outcome — e.g. non-UK destinations at/above threshold in one row (such as {Ireland, Other} or {Ireland, International}), or UK at/above threshold in one row ({£50, £75}). Not enumerated as separate rows per destination or per order value when the result is identical.
assertions.evidence: Express rows consolidate: 'Express – below threshold' groups {UK, Ireland, EU, International} at £30 into one row; 'Express – above threshold, UK' uses value set {£75} (but paired with earlier £50 row); 'Express – at or above threshold, non-UK (no free tier)' groups {Ireland, EU, International} at {£50, £75} = £9.99 in one row. Value sets are used to consolidate identical outcomes.

assertions.text: Overnight UK and Ireland are in one row using a value set ({UK, Ireland}) — not separate rows, since both have the same cost and availability.
assertions.evidence: In the 'Shipping Method Availability' table, Overnight UK and Ireland are shown as separate rows: 'Overnight – UK' (UK, yes) and 'Overnight – Ireland' (Ireland, yes). Although the cost table correctly shows 'Overnight – UK or Ireland, any value' in one row, the availability table violates the principle by splitting them into separate rows despite identical outcomes.

assertions.text: Standard shipping destination uses a value set covering all options (e.g. {UK, Ireland, International} or {UK, Ireland, Other}) or is blank/absent — either approach is valid since destination is irrelevant to the cost.
assertions.evidence: Standard shipping row shows: 'Standard – fixed rate, any destination or value' | {UK, Ireland, EU, International} | {£20, £75} | £3.99. Destination is represented as a value set covering all options.

assertions.text: At least one output column ends with '?'
assertions.evidence: The first table has column header 'Available?' and the second table has column header 'Cost?' — both output columns end with question marks.

assertions.text: Cell values use concrete domain terms (e.g. 'Standard', 'Express', 'UK', '£3.99') — not abstract codes or raw booleans like 'true', 'false', 'TYPE_1', '1'.
assertions.evidence: Cell values throughout both tables use concrete domain terms: shipping methods ('Standard', 'Express', 'Overnight'), destinations ('UK', 'Ireland', 'EU', 'International'), currency amounts ('£3.99', '£9.99', '£0.00', '£30', '£49.99', '£50', '£75'), and availability labels ('yes', 'no' rather than boolean true/false).

assertions.text: Value sets (not blanks) are used for irrelevant inputs — e.g. Standard shipping destination uses a value set like {UK, Ireland, International} because destination exists but doesn't affect the cost. Blanks are reserved for genuinely absent/N/A inputs. The distinction between 'irrelevant to this rule' (value set) and 'not applicable' (blank) is correct.
assertions.evidence: Standard destination uses value set {UK, Ireland, EU, International} correctly, as destination exists but is irrelevant to the fixed £3.99 cost. Overnight unavailable for EU/International is shown with value set {EU, International} | no in the availability table (irrelevant input with consistent outcome), not a blank. The tables correctly distinguish irrelevant-but-present inputs (value sets) from genuinely absent inputs.
